name: SVS SB-1000 Pro
summary: A compact sealed 12-inch sub with a 325 W RMS amp and app-based EQ that suits rooms up to about 2,000 cubic feet and blends easily with music and movies.
verdict:
The SB-1000 Pro puts a **12-inch driver** in a compact **sealed** cabinet, driven by a **325 W RMS (820 W peak)** amplifier. SVS rates it at **20–270 Hz ±3 dB**.

Start with the room. Multiply length × width × height: a 14 × 18 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling is **2,016 cu ft**. As a rough guide, a good sealed 12-inch sub covers rooms up to about 2,000 cu ft at movie levels. Above that, or in an open-plan space, a ported model or a second sub is the better plan.

Why a 12-inch over a 10-inch? Cone area scales with the square of diameter, so (12 ÷ 10)² = **1.44×** the area. At the same cone travel, that is about 20 × log10(1.44) = **3 dB** more output. And bass gets harder as it goes lower: to hold the same level an octave down, the cone must move **four times** as much air. A sealed box gives up some of that deep output in exchange for a smaller cabinet and a gentle roll-off that blends well with natural room gain.

The **SVS app** (over Bluetooth) handles [crossover](/glossary/crossover/), phase, parametric EQ and room gain compensation from your seat. If your room is bigger than 2,000 cu ft, look at the ported [SVS PB-1000 Pro](/gear/svs-pb-1000-pro/). See our [best subwoofer for home theater](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) guide for the full ranking.

name: SVS PB-1000 Pro
summary: The ported sibling of the SB-1000 Pro, with the same 12-inch driver and 325 W RMS amp but deeper extension to 18 Hz and selectable port tuning, for rooms up to about 3,000 cubic feet.
verdict:
The PB-1000 Pro uses the same **12-inch driver** and **325 W RMS (820 W peak)** amp as the [SB-1000 Pro](/gear/svs-sb-1000-pro/), but in a larger **ported** cabinet. SVS rates it at **18–270 Hz ±3 dB**, 2 Hz deeper than the sealed version.

That 2 Hz matters more than it looks. To play the same level at 18 Hz as at 36 Hz, a driver must move **four times** the air. A port tuned low adds output right where the cone struggles, so on paper the PB-1000 Pro plays louder in the deepest octave, where explosions and rumble live.

Room maths: a 15 × 20 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling is **2,400 cu ft**. As a rough guide, a single ported 12-inch sub like this covers rooms up to about 3,000 cu ft at movie levels. Beyond that, plan for two subs; two identical subs placed together can add up to about **6 dB**.

The app lets you switch between **three tuning modes**, including a sealed mode, so you can trade some deep output for a tighter roll-off. It also handles [crossover](/glossary/crossover/), phase and parametric EQ.

The cost is size: the cabinet is much bigger than the sealed model. If you have the floor space, it is one of the best-value movie subs in our [best subwoofer for home theater](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) guide.

The PL-200 II packs a **12-inch driver** and a **250 W RMS** amp, with BIC quoting **1,000 W peak**. That peak figure is a good place to do the maths. Peak ratings describe brief bursts, not continuous output, and the gap between 250 W and 1,000 W is a 4× ratio, or **6 dB**. You will not get 6 dB more bass from a peak rating, so compare subs on RMS power only.

On RMS, it stacks up well. Against the 200 W [Klipsch R-120SW](/gear/klipsch-r-120sw/), 10 × log10(250 ÷ 200) = about **1 dB** more amp headroom. Against the 100 W [Polk Monitor XT12](/gear/polk-monitor-xt12/), it is about **4 dB** more.

Room maths: a 14 × 16 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling is **1,792 cu ft**. As a rough guide, a 12-inch budget sub with a 250 W amp suits rooms up to about **2,000 cu ft**. The 12-inch cone has (12 ÷ 10)² = 1.44× the area of a 10-inch, about 3 dB more output at the same cone travel.

There is no app or EQ, so use your receiver's [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/) and set the [crossover](/glossary/crossover/) at 80 Hz. For the money, owners report it plays louder than most budget rivals. Compare it in our [best budget subwoofer for home theater](/best-budget-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) guide.

name: Dayton Audio SUB-1200
summary: One of the cheapest 12-inch subs from a known brand, with a 100 W RMS amp and both line- and speaker-level inputs, for small and medium rooms on a tight budget.
verdict:
The SUB-1200 is a **12-inch** sub with a **100 W RMS** amp at a price many brands charge for a 10-inch. Dayton rates it at **25–140 Hz**.

The driver size is the value story. Cone area scales with the square of diameter: (12 ÷ 10)² = **1.44×** the area of a 10-inch, about 3 dB more output at the same cone travel. That is the same gain as doubling amp power, for free.

The amp is the limit. Compared with a 200 W sub like the [Klipsch R-120SW](/gear/klipsch-r-120sw/), 10 × log10(200 ÷ 100) = **3 dB** less headroom. In practice that means the SUB-1200 sounds full at moderate levels but compresses on big movie effects in a larger room.

Room maths: a 12 × 14 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling is **1,344 cu ft**. As a rough guide, this sub suits rooms up to about **1,500 cu ft**. Its 25 Hz lower limit is a broad manufacturer figure, so expect the deepest notes to be lighter than on SVS subs rated at ±3 dB.

It has both line-level and speaker-level inputs, so it works with receivers and older stereo amps. Set your [crossover](/glossary/crossover/) to 80 Hz and run your receiver's [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/). It is a solid choice in our [best budget subwoofer for home theater](/best-budget-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) guide.

name: ELAC Debut 3030 Subwoofer
summary: A 12-inch ELAC Debut sub whose standout feature is app-based Auto EQ, which helps tame room modes even if your receiver's correction is basic.
verdict:
The Debut SUB3030 is a **12-inch** sub whose best feature is software: ELAC's **SUB Control app** connects over Bluetooth and runs an **Auto EQ** routine using your phone. We have not listed amp power or frequency response here because we could not confirm ELAC's figures; check the listing before comparing output with SVS or Klipsch rivals.

Why Auto EQ matters: in a typical room, standing waves can create bass peaks of 10 dB or more at some seats and deep dips at others. A 10 dB peak means one note sounds about twice as loud as its neighbors. Cutting those peaks with EQ costs nothing in headroom and makes the whole system sound tighter, which is why [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/) often matters more than raw watts. If your receiver has only basic correction, like the [Yamaha RX-V6A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v6a/)'s YPAO, a sub with its own EQ fills the gap.

Room maths: a 13 × 16 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling is **1,664 cu ft**. As a rough guide, a single 12-inch sub suits rooms up to about **1,500–2,000 cu ft**. A 12-inch cone has (12 ÷ 10)² = 1.44× the area of a 10-inch, about 3 dB more output at the same cone travel.

Set your receiver's [crossover](/glossary/crossover/) at 80 Hz, then run Auto EQ from the main seat. Compare it in our [best subwoofer for home theater](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) guide.

Its signature is REL's **high-level (Neutrik Speakon) input**, which takes signal from your amplifier's speaker terminals so the sub hears the same signal as your main speakers.

That design is aimed at music. For home theater, the maths says it is a small-room sub. An 8-inch driver has (8 ÷ 12)² = **0.44×** the cone area of a 12-inch, about 7 dB less output at the same cone travel. The passive radiator helps with deep extension by adding radiating area without a port, but it does not change the basic displacement limit.

Room maths: an 11 × 13 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling is **1,144 cu ft**. As a rough guide, the T/5x suits rooms up to about **1,200 cu ft**, or larger rooms as one of a pair. Two subs placed together can add up to about 6 dB, and REL owners often run two for stereo bass.

In a home theater, connect the [LFE](/glossary/lfe/) input for movies and the high-level input for music, then set the sub's own [crossover](/glossary/crossover/) low so it only fills in the bottom octave. For movie-first rooms, the [SVS SB-1000 Pro](/gear/svs-sb-1000-pro/) gives much more output for the money. verdict:
The Sub 4 uses **two force-canceling woofers** mounted face to face, each driven by its own Class D amp, so cabinet vibration cancels out. Sonos says it plays down to **25 Hz**. It connects over Wi-Fi to Sonos soundbars and speakers like the [Sonos Arc Ultra](/gear/sonos-arc-ultra/), with no cable to the TV.

Here is the maths to weigh. Sonos does not publish driver size or amp power, so you cannot compare output on paper with a 12-inch [SVS SB-1000 Pro](/gear/svs-sb-1000-pro/). What you can compare is extension: 25 Hz versus the SVS's 20 Hz is about a third of an octave, and the cone must move roughly **1.6×** as much air to hold the same level at 20 Hz as at 25 Hz.

Room maths: a 14 × 16 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling is **1,792 cu ft**. As a rough guide, one Sub 4 suits living rooms up to around that size. Sonos lets some systems pair a second sub; two subs placed together can add up to about 6 dB.

The real value is integration: Trueplay tuning, automatic crossover and setup in the Sonos app. The catch is that it works **only** with Sonos. If you are building a receiver-based system, a wired sub gives more bass per dollar.
